summary.text: 火 is an indivisible picture of rising flames, used to write the word ‘fire’.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts rising flames; it is not built from smaller semantic or phonetic components.

components.text: The entire graph pictures rising flames and represents fire. It has no smaller components; no part supplies a sound cue.

history.text: The curated Shang oracle-bone examples show different forms of 火, illustrating variation without establishing a sequence between them. Warring States forms are described as more linear, with a stroke reversed and a horizontal added. The cited collection contains no bronze form, which does not prove that no bronze example exists elsewhere.
A Han-period lexicographic account also describes flames rising and classifies 火 as a pictogram; this is a later explanation, not direct evidence for the Shang graph’s origin.

uncertainties.text: The cited oracle-bone examples establish Shang-period use, but their individual dates are unresolved. The selected images are modern vector renderings of catalogued forms, not artifact photographs.
Competing Old Chinese reconstructions and proposed inherited comparisons remain unresolved; the proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison is specifically described as phonologically problematic.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; individual inscription dates unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples include 火 in a literal fire context; the graph is analyzed as a picture of rising flames.

senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; also attested in the Classic of Poetry
senses.text: 火 is attested as a name for 大火, identified with Antares. The reason for the star’s name is not established.
‘Burn’ is listed as a gloss, but its date and historical relation to ‘fire’ are unresolved.
‘Anger’ and ‘rage’ are listed as glosses, but their dates and historical relation to ‘fire’ are unresolved.

limitations.text: The star-name is attested separately, with no supported semantic path linking it to literal ‘fire’.
The supplied glosses do not establish when ‘burn’ or ‘anger/rage’ arose or how they relate to ‘fire’.

One interpretation reads 火 in an oracle-bone context as a phonetic loan for 禍 ‘calamity’: the sign would have been reused for a different word because the words were thought to sound similar. The proposal is based on sound proximity and context, but no independently checked sound comparison is supplied.

overview.text: 火 is a whole-character picture of rising flames representing fire. It has no smaller sound or meaning parts.

components.text: Read the whole graph as a picture of rising flames representing fire; it has no smaller component parts.

limitations.text: These are modern vector renderings of glyphs catalogued from oracle-bone records, not photographs of artifacts. The cited examples are Shang-period, but their individual archaeological dates are not established here.
The rising-flame reading is a scholarly analysis of the graph; the shapes alone do not establish its historical meaning.
